tagline: A silver-mining supply road crosses the Sierra on narrow pavement.
intro: The Ebbetts Pass Scenic Byway crosses the Sierra Nevada on 61 miles of California Highways 4 and 89, through Arnold, Bear Valley and Markleeville. Two-lane pavement at either end narrows into a steep, curving single lane higher up. The Federal Highway Administration lists it as a National Scenic Byway, highlighting glacial valleys, volcanic peaks and granite ridges, and allows two hours to drive it. The route traverses two national forests and two wilderness areas, with state parks anchoring its ends.

John Ebbetts considered a railroad crossing here, but his survey near the pass found the route unsuitable. Ebbetts had intended another survey for a road, but died in a steamboat explosion in 1854 before he could return. Silver discoveries east of the Sierra gave the crossing another purpose: merchants in Murphys commissioned a road to Markleeville to carry supplies to the miners. It became a toll road in 1862.

From Arnold, the drive runs through Dorrington toward Bear Valley. Highway 4 passes north of Lake Alpine before crossing Pacific Grade Summit and then Ebbetts Pass. Beyond the Mount Reba turnoff, the pavement loses its center line and the curves tighten into switchbacks. Highway 4 then descends to Highway 89 near Markleeville, the community at the byway’s eastern end.

moments.title: Arnold
moments.text: Arnold takes its name from Bob and Bernice Arnold, who opened the Ebbetts Pass Inn in 1927. Before their inn, the community consisted of two large ranches, with logging as its main industry. The inn served travelers on the pass route and people visiting nearby Calaveras Big Trees State Park. A post office followed in 1934, and Bernice served as postmistress. The town lies on State Route 4 in Stanislaus National Forest, with White Pines Park and Calaveras Big Trees among the parks in the area. The Arnold Rim Trail, created in 2007, links Arnold and Avery across protected land.

moments.title: Lake Alpine
moments.text: Lake Alpine is a reservoir formed by Alpine Dam on Silver Creek, east of Bear Valley. It sits at 7,303 feet, with Highway 4 running north of the water between Bear Valley and Pacific Grade Summit. The community on its north shore consists of cabins authorized by the United States Forest Service under the Occupancy Permits Act.
moments.notice: Highway 4 follows the north side of the reservoir.

moments.title: Ebbetts Pass
moments.text: At Ebbetts Pass, the Pacific Crest Trail crosses State Route 4. This is the eastern of the road’s two passes; Pacific Grade Summit lies to the west. Between Lake Alpine and Centerville Flat, a 23-mile section is less than two lanes wide and has no dividing line. On the eastern slope, many hairpins are blind and grow abruptly steeper at the apex. The pass had carried Ebbetts’s name before the U.S. Geological Survey made it official during its 1893 survey of the Markleeville quadrangle. National Scenic Byway status arrived on September 22, 2005.
moments.notice: The Pacific Crest Trail crosses Highway 4 at the pass.

practical: Ebbetts Pass: The high road closes in winter. The byway association advises checking road conditions before travel. (checked 2026-10-11)
